about: Notes for folio-eval --cards, which writes flashcards from each with the on-device AI and reports how many were kept, how many were dropped and why, and how long it took. All text is original sample content. expectsCards false marks text with few answers in it, such as a past paper's questions.

notes.subject: Physics
notes.text:
Electromagnetic induction
Magnetic flux Φ is the product of the magnetic field strength and the area perpendicular to it: Φ = B⊥A. It is measured in webers (Wb).
Faraday's law: an emf is induced in a conductor when the magnetic flux through it changes. The size of the induced emf equals the rate of change of flux linkage: ε = −N ΔΦ/Δt, where N is the number of turns in the coil.
Lenz's law: the induced current flows in a direction that creates a magnetic field opposing the change in flux that produced it. This is why the equation has a negative sign, and it follows from the conservation of energy.
Eddy currents are loops of current induced in a solid conductor moving through a magnetic field, or in a changing field. They oppose the motion, which is used in magnetic braking on trains and roller coasters.
Transformers change the size of an alternating voltage. An alternating current in the primary coil creates a changing flux in the iron core, which induces an emf in the secondary coil. For an ideal transformer, Vp/Vs = Np/Ns, and the power in equals the power out, so VpIp = VsIs.
A step-up transformer has more turns on the secondary coil than the primary. Power stations use step-up transformers so electricity is transmitted at high voltage and low current, which reduces energy lost as heat in the wires (P = I²R).
Real transformers lose energy through eddy currents in the core, which is why cores are laminated, and through resistance heating in the coils.
AC generators turn a coil in a magnetic field. The flux through the coil changes continuously, so an alternating emf is induced. Slip rings keep the connection to the external circuit. A DC generator uses a split ring commutator instead, which reverses the connection every half turn.

notes.subject: Chemistry
notes.text:
Acid/base reactions
The Brønsted–Lowry theory defines an acid as a proton (H⁺) donor and a base as a proton acceptor. When an acid donates a proton, what remains is its conjugate base; for example, the conjugate base of HCl is Cl⁻.
Strong acids, such as hydrochloric, nitric and sulfuric acid, ionise completely in water. Weak acids, such as ethanoic acid and citric acid, only partially ionise, so an equilibrium forms.
pH = −log₁₀[H₃O⁺]. A solution with pH 7 is neutral at 25 °C; each decrease of one pH unit is a tenfold increase in hydronium ion concentration.
pH + pOH = 14 at 25 °C, because Kw = [H₃O⁺][OH⁻] = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴.
The acid dissociation constant Ka measures the strength of a weak acid. A larger Ka means a stronger acid; pKa = −log₁₀Ka.
A buffer is a solution that resists changes in pH when small amounts of acid or base are added. It contains a weak acid and its conjugate base in similar amounts, such as ethanoic acid and sodium ethanoate. Blood is buffered by carbonic acid and hydrogen carbonate ions.
In a titration, a solution of known concentration (the standard solution) is added from a burette until the equivalence point is reached. An indicator changes colour at the end point; phenolphthalein is used for titrations of a weak acid with a strong base because its colour change happens at about pH 8.2 to 10.
A primary standard must be pure, stable, have a high molar mass and not absorb water from the air. Anhydrous sodium carbonate is a common primary standard.

notes.subject: Biology
notes.text:
DNA and replication
DNA is a double helix made of two strands of nucleotides. Each nucleotide has a phosphate group, a deoxyribose sugar and one of four nitrogenous bases: adenine, thymine, guanine and cytosine.
The bases pair by hydrogen bonds: adenine with thymine and guanine with cytosine. This is called complementary base pairing.
DNA replication is semi-conservative: each new DNA molecule contains one original strand and one newly made strand. Meselson and Stahl showed this in 1958 using heavy nitrogen.
Replication begins when the enzyme helicase unwinds the double helix and breaks the hydrogen bonds between the bases. DNA polymerase then adds free nucleotides to each template strand, building the new strand in the 5′ to 3′ direction.
Because the strands are antiparallel, the leading strand is made continuously, while the lagging strand is made in short pieces called Okazaki fragments. DNA ligase joins these fragments together.
Mutations are changes in the DNA sequence. A point mutation changes a single base and may be silent, missense or nonsense. Mutagens such as UV radiation and some chemicals increase the rate of mutation.

notes.subject: Modern History
notes.text:
Nazi Germany: consolidating power, 1933–1934
Hitler was appointed Chancellor on 30 January 1933 by President Hindenburg. Conservative politicians such as Franz von Papen believed they could control him.
On 27 February 1933 the Reichstag building was set on fire. The Nazis blamed the communists, and the Reichstag Fire Decree suspended civil liberties such as freedom of speech and of the press.
The Enabling Act, passed on 23 March 1933, allowed Hitler's cabinet to make laws without the Reichstag for four years. It effectively ended parliamentary democracy in Germany.
Through Gleichschaltung (coordination), the Nazis brought institutions under their control. Trade unions were abolished in May 1933 and replaced by the German Labour Front. By July 1933 all other political parties had been banned.
In the Night of the Long Knives (30 June – 2 July 1934), the SS murdered Ernst Röhm and other SA leaders, as well as political opponents. This removed a threat from within the party and won the support of the army.
When Hindenburg died on 2 August 1934, Hitler combined the offices of Chancellor and President and took the title Führer. The army swore an oath of personal loyalty to him.
Propaganda, directed by Joseph Goebbels, controlled newspapers, radio and film, while the Gestapo used terror and informers to silence opposition. The first concentration camp, Dachau, opened in March 1933 for political prisoners.

notes.subject: English Advanced
notes.text:
Macbeth: key themes and quotations
Ambition: Macbeth's 'vaulting ambition, which o'erleaps itself' drives him to murder King Duncan. Shakespeare shows that ambition without moral limits leads to destruction.
The supernatural: the three witches prophesy that Macbeth will be Thane of Cawdor and king. Their equivocal language, 'Fair is foul, and foul is fair', blurs the line between good and evil.
Guilt: after the murder Macbeth says 'Will all great Neptune's ocean wash this blood / Clean from my hand?' Lady Macbeth later sleepwalks and tries to wash imaginary blood from her hands, crying 'Out, damned spot!'
Kingship: Duncan and Edward the Confessor represent good kingship, while Macbeth becomes a tyrant. Malcolm tests Macduff's loyalty in Act 4 Scene 3.
Appearance and reality: Duncan admits 'There's no art / To find the mind's construction in the face', just before he trusts Macbeth. Lady Macbeth tells her husband to 'look like th' innocent flower, / But be the serpent under't'.
Gender: Lady Macbeth calls on spirits to 'unsex me here' and questions Macbeth's manhood to push him to kill.
The play ends with Macduff killing Macbeth, revealing he was 'from his mother's womb / Untimely ripped', which fulfils the witches' prophecy.

notes.subject: Mathematics Advanced
notes.text:
Differentiation rules
The derivative f′(x) gives the gradient of the tangent to y = f(x) at any point and the instantaneous rate of change.
Power rule: if y = xⁿ, then dy/dx = nxⁿ⁻¹. For example, the derivative of x⁵ is 5x⁴.
Product rule: if y = uv, then dy/dx = u′v + uv′.
Quotient rule: if y = u/v, then dy/dx = (u′v − uv′)/v².
Chain rule: if y = f(g(x)), then dy/dx = f′(g(x)) × g′(x). For example, the derivative of (3x + 1)⁴ is 12(3x + 1)³.
The derivative of eˣ is eˣ, the derivative of ln x is 1/x, the derivative of sin x is cos x, and the derivative of cos x is −sin x.
Stationary points occur where f′(x) = 0. If f″(x) > 0 the point is a local minimum; if f″(x) < 0 it is a local maximum. A point of inflection is where the concavity changes, which happens where f″(x) = 0 and the sign of f″(x) changes.

notes.subject: Studies of Religion I
notes.text:
Religious expression in Australia since 1945
The 1947 census showed that about 88 per cent of Australians identified as Christian, most of them Anglican or Catholic.
Post-war immigration from Europe increased the number of Catholics and Orthodox Christians, and the end of the White Australia Policy in 1973 allowed migrants from Asia and the Middle East, increasing the number of Buddhists, Hindus and Muslims.
Religious diversity grew further with the arrival of refugees, and by the 2021 census Islam and Hinduism were among the fastest-growing religions.
Secularism also increased. 'No religion' was the largest single response in the 2021 census, at about 39 per cent.
Ecumenism is the movement towards unity among Christian denominations. The Uniting Church was formed in 1977 from Methodist, Presbyterian and Congregational churches. The National Council of Churches in Australia was formed in 1994.
Interfaith dialogue brings different religious traditions together to build understanding.
Aboriginal spiritualities are based on the Dreaming, which links people, land and kinship. Dispossession and the separation of children from their families disconnected many Aboriginal people from the land and their spirituality.

notes.subject: Music 1
notes.text:
The concepts of music
Duration is about time in music: beat, rhythm, tempo and metre. A time signature such as 3/4 shows three crotchet beats in each bar.
Pitch describes how high or low a sound is, including melody, harmony and tonality. A melody that moves by step is conjunct; one that leaps is disjunct.
Dynamics and expressive techniques include volume, such as piano (soft) and forte (loud), crescendo and diminuendo, and articulation such as staccato and legato.
Tone colour, or timbre, is the unique quality of a sound, which depends on the instrument and how it is played, such as pizzicato strings or a muted trumpet.
Texture is how layers of sound combine. Monophonic texture is a single melody line, homophonic is a melody with accompaniment, and polyphonic is several independent melodies at once.
Structure is the form of a piece, such as binary form (AB), ternary form (ABA), rondo (ABACA) and verse–chorus form in popular music.

notes.subject: Chinese Continuers
notes.text:
把字句
把字句用来强调动作对宾语的处理或影响。结构是：主语＋把＋宾语＋动词＋其他成分。例如：我把作业做完了。
动词后面一定要有其他成分，比如结果补语、趋向补语或者“了”。不能说“我把苹果吃”。
了
“了”放在动词后面表示动作已经完成，例如：我吃了早饭。
“了”放在句子末尾表示情况发生了变化，例如：天冷了。
量词
汉语的名词前面要用量词。一本书，一张纸，一只猫，一条河，一件衣服。
“个”是最常用的量词，可以用在很多名词前面，比如一个人、一个苹果。

notes.subject: History
notes.text:
La Révolution française
En 1789, la France connaît une grave crise financière. Pour trouver de nouveaux impôts, Louis XVI convoque les États généraux à Versailles en mai 1789.
Le 17 juin, les députés du tiers état se proclament Assemblée nationale. Le 20 juin, ils prêtent le serment du Jeu de paume et jurent de donner une constitution à la France.
Le 14 juillet 1789, le peuple de Paris prend la Bastille, une prison qui symbolise le pouvoir absolu du roi.
Dans la nuit du 4 août, l'Assemblée abolit les privilèges de la noblesse et du clergé. Le 26 août, elle adopte la Déclaration des droits de l'homme et du citoyen.
En 1792, la monarchie est abolie et la Première République est proclamée. Louis XVI est exécuté en janvier 1793.
De 1793 à 1794, sous la Terreur, Robespierre et le Comité de salut public font exécuter des milliers d'opposants.

notes.subject: Economics
notes.text:
Demand and supply
The law of demand states that, other things being equal, as the price of a good rises the quantity demanded falls. This is shown by a downward-sloping demand curve.
The law of supply states that as price rises the quantity supplied rises, because producers can make more profit.
Equilibrium price is where the quantity demanded equals the quantity supplied. If the price is above equilibrium there is a surplus; if it is below equilibrium there is a shortage.
A change in price causes a movement along the curve. A change in another factor, such as income, tastes or the price of a substitute, shifts the whole demand curve.
Price elasticity of demand measures how responsive quantity demanded is to a change in price. Demand is elastic if the percentage change in quantity is greater than the percentage change in price. Necessities such as petrol tend to be price inelastic.

notes.subject: Chemistry
notes.text:
Organic chemistry summary
Hydrocarbons
Alkanes are saturated hydrocarbons with only single carbon–carbon bonds and the general formula CₙH₂ₙ₊₂. Alkenes contain at least one carbon–carbon double bond and have the general formula CₙH₂ₙ. Alkynes contain a triple bond.
The boiling points of alkanes increase with chain length because the dispersion forces between longer molecules are stronger.
Naming
Organic compounds are named using IUPAC rules: find the longest chain containing the functional group, number it so the functional group has the lowest number, and name branches in alphabetical order.
Structural isomers have the same molecular formula but different structures. Chain isomers differ in branching, position isomers in where the functional group is, and functional group isomers have different functional groups, such as propanal and propanone.
Functional groups
Alcohols contain the hydroxyl group (–OH) and end in -ol. Aldehydes and ketones contain the carbonyl group; aldehydes end in -al and ketones in -one. Carboxylic acids contain the carboxyl group (–COOH) and end in -oic acid. Esters end in -oate, amines contain the –NH₂ group and amides contain –CONH₂.
Alcohols have higher boiling points than alkanes of similar mass because their molecules form hydrogen bonds. Short-chain alcohols are soluble in water, but solubility falls as the hydrocarbon chain gets longer.
Reactions of alkenes
Alkenes undergo addition reactions because of their double bond. With hydrogen and a nickel catalyst they form alkanes (hydrogenation). With bromine water they form dibromoalkanes, and the bromine water changes from orange to colourless, which is the test for unsaturation. With water and an acid catalyst they form alcohols (hydration).
Alkanes react with halogens by substitution, which needs ultraviolet light.
Reactions of alcohols
Primary alcohols are oxidised by acidified potassium dichromate to aldehydes and then to carboxylic acids. Secondary alcohols are oxidised to ketones. Tertiary alcohols are not easily oxidised. The dichromate changes from orange to green when an oxidation happens.
Alcohols can be dehydrated with concentrated sulfuric acid to form alkenes. Complete combustion of an alcohol produces carbon dioxide and water.
Esterification
A carboxylic acid and an alcohol react to form an ester and water, using concentrated sulfuric acid as a catalyst. The mixture is heated under reflux so volatile reactants and products condense and return to the flask instead of escaping. Esters have fruity smells and are used in flavourings and perfumes.
Polymers
Addition polymers form when many alkene monomers join, such as ethene forming polyethylene. Low-density polyethylene has branched chains, while high-density polyethylene has straight chains that pack closely, so it is stronger and more rigid.
Condensation polymers form when monomers join and release a small molecule, usually water. Polyesters such as PET form from a diol and a dicarboxylic acid, and nylon is a polyamide.
Soaps and detergents
Soaps are made by saponification: a fat or oil is heated with sodium hydroxide to form glycerol and the sodium salts of fatty acids. A soap particle has a hydrophilic ionic head and a long hydrophobic tail, so it can surround grease to form a micelle. Detergents work in the same way but do not form scum in hard water.
